tip: Dutch names things with 'heten', not 'to be': Hoe heet je? literally asks how you are called.
In 'waar kom je vandaan?', vandaan breaks off and lands at the end: waar ... vandaan = where ... from.
'Kind' has an irregular plural in -eren: one kind, several kinderen.
'Hoe gaat het met ...?' is the set way to ask how someone is doing: gaat het met je familie.
'Praten' takes 'over' for the topic: praat over haar werk = talks about her work.
'Deze' is the 'this' for de-words: de stoel becomes deze stoel.
After a number, measure nouns stay singular: twee uur = two hours, never 'twee uren'.
De-words take -e on the adjective even after 'een': de wijnkaart, so een mooie wijnkaart.
Start with a time word and the verb still comes second, before the subject: Gisteren heb ik.
Days of the week take 'op': op zaterdag = on Saturday.
A modal like 'moet' pushes the other verb to the end as an infinitive: moet je stil zijn.
In an indirect question the verb goes to the very end: hoe oud je bent, not 'hoe oud bent je'.
Verbs of motion build the perfect with 'zijn', not 'hebben': is ... aangekomen = has arrived.
A separable verb tucks -ge- inside its participle: thuiskomen becomes thuisgekomen.
Verbs starting with be-, ver-, ont- skip the ge- in the participle: betalen becomes betaald.
'Om ... te' plus an infinitive means 'in order to': om wakker te worden = to wake up.
When 'je' follows the verb, drop the -t: kun je, not 'kunt je'.
Weather uses a dummy 'het' with no real subject: het regent = it rains.
'Liever' is how you say you would rather: wil ik liever thuisblijven = I'd rather stay home.
'Erbij' is er + bij, meaning 'with it': een glas kraanwater erbij = a tap water with it.
An infinitive can work as a noun: bewegen here means moving, the activity itself.
Dutch glues compounds into one word: pepermunt plus thee becomes pepermuntthee.
Before a noun 'heel' inflects to 'hele' for 'whole': het hele dak = the entire roof.
In the main clause a separable verb splits, its prefix moving to the end: bieden ... aan.
The -tje ending makes a diminutive, always a het-word: tuintje = little garden.
Strong verbs change their vowel in the participle: drinken becomes gedronken.
A double vowel drops to one when the adjective adds -e: groot becomes grote.
